symptoms: Minutes after a fraud-scorer release finished rolling, CPU rose on both pods, the throttling view went past 25%, and payments-api logged PAYAPI-W0310 for late fraud scores.

# Two logout waves from one auth-service release

team-identity · sev2 · 2026-07-21, 14:05 to 14:30 UTC · runbooks: RB-026, RB-018

## What users went through

Twice in one afternoon signed-in users were sent back to the login page. The first wave came
from sessions created before the release, the second from sessions created while the release was
serving. Signing in again worked both times.

## What the release changed

This release altered how auth-service serializes session values kept in redis-sessions, keys
beginning `sess:`. Code from the release couldn't decode a value written by the previous build,
and the previous build couldn't decode one written by the release. When a value won't decode,
the lookup fails like any missing session would: `AUTH-E401X`, and the user goes to sign in.

We roll auth-service with stock Deployment settings, adding a pod before removing one. So for
several minutes both builds served traffic, and users whose requests hopped between builds were
signed out.

## Timeline (UTC)

- 14:05 rollout starts.
- 14:08 first pod of the release Ready. `AUTH-E401X` climbs immediately.
- 14:11 auth-service-01 and auth-service-02 both run the release. Sessions from before it can
  no longer be read.
- 14:14 paged on the `AUTH-E401X` rate.
- 14:16 Redis ruled out first, using RB-018's checks: same sessions primary as this morning, and
  auth-service had logged no failed session writes. No failover.
- 14:17 RB-026: errors started as that first pod went Ready, and this release touched stored
  session data, which is where rolling back stops being free.
- 14:20 rolled back with `kubectl rollout undo`.
- 14:23 a pod on the previous build is serving again. Users who signed in during the release
  start failing.
- 14:30 that second wave has faded; resolved.

## Why one release made two waves

Each wave was sessions written by one build meeting a reader from the other. Moving forward
stranded sessions created before 14:08. Moving back stranded those created between 14:08 and the
rollback. Rolling back didn't end anything; it changed which group of users paid.

## What was kept

The session values stayed in redis-sessions, unreadable rather than deleted: neither build could
interpret the other's. What users paid was forced sign-ins.

## Was rolling back right?

At 14:20 it felt safe. It wasn't cheaper. RB-026 asks, whenever a release changes stored data,
whether older code understands what newer code wrote. Here it did not. Had we stayed put and
shipped a build that decodes both encodings, people who signed in after 14:08 would have kept
their sessions. That build shipped one day later, 2026-07-22.

## Changes we are making

1. Release review flags any change to persisted formats: session values, cache keys, message
   bodies. Such changes ship in two steps: first a reader for both formats, later the new writer.
2. A dashboard panel splitting `AUTH-E401X` by ReplicaSet, so a glance shows whether errors sit
   on one build.
resolution: Rolled back at 14:20; the second wave, from sessions created by the release, faded by 14:30, and a build able to decode both encodings shipped on 2026-07-22.
root_cause: The auth-service release changed how session values stored under sess: in redis-sessions were encoded, and neither build could decode values written by the other.
symptoms: AUTH-E401X jumped at 14:08 when the first pod of the release turned Ready, and again from 14:23 after the rollback, on auth-service-01 and auth-service-02.
title: Session encoding change logged users out twice

# search-cluster-01, Sunday 9 August 2026: clock log from search on-call

sev4. Runbook RB-008. Host search-cluster-01.prod.internal. All times UTC.

**00:50** Queue sweep turns up a `/var` warning on search-cluster-01. This check raises a ticket at 90%, never a page, which is why it came to me by reading rather than by a phone buzzing. The reading has crept higher since it was raised.

**00:53** Is search hurting? Queries against `products` through `search-cluster-01.prod.internal:9200` come back at their usual pace. Shards sit on a separate volume, so a crowded root filesystem threatens logging and the OS long before it threatens the index.

**00:58** Root filesystem: 40 GB, the standard size. Ordinarily about 11 GB of it is occupied. At this moment, more than nine tenths.

**01:02** Hunch: OpenSearch's log folder. One of its files once went unrotated on this cluster and swallowed a node, so that's where I look.

**01:07** Hunch wrong. `/etc/logrotate.d/` has its OpenSearch entry, live files are tiny, and compressed archives are few.

**01:12** Step back and measure everything in `/var` using `du`. Biggest by far: the systemd journal directory.

**01:16** journald's own size report matches. Its config file holds no size directive whatsoever.

**01:21** Any deleted-but-open files? `lsof +L1` lists none. The journal is the only thing to trim.

**01:24** Vacuum the journal down to 500M; journald drops its oldest archives first.

**01:26** Occupied space falls back to roughly the normal 11 GB. The next check clears the ticket condition.

**01:34** `SystemMaxUse=500M` goes into `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` under `[Journal]`; journald gets restarted. Its reported size now stays beneath that ceiling.

**01:40** Glance at OpenSearch output on search-cluster-01 to confirm the journald restart disturbed nothing. Lines flowing as normal.

**02:00** Flat. Holding it open longer, since the original climb was gradual and one reading proves little.

**02:25** Still flat. Done, 95 minutes after I picked it up.

**For daytime**

- One lesson rather than a to-do list: chasing last time's culprit first cost a few minutes. Measure all of `/var`, then follow the largest directory.
resolution: Vacuumed the journal to 500M and set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf on search-cluster-01, then restarted journald; /var returned to about 11 GB used.
root_cause: search-cluster-01 had no journald size limit, so the systemd journal under /var/log/journal grew until it held most of the 40 GB root disk.
symptoms: A /var-over-90% ticket for search-cluster-01 was rising after midnight; OpenSearch logs were rotating normally and search kept working.
title: search-cluster-01 journal outgrew its root disk share

# Two Kafka brokers refused a pushed config

sev2 · 2026-08-13 · 10:12 to 10:36 UTC · cause: kafka · affected: ledger-service, orders-api · runbook: RB-027

| Host or team | UTC | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| kafka-01 | 10:12 | Picked as the canary. The tool replaced `server.properties`, restarted the broker and got exit code 0. A few seconds later the JVM quit with a `ConfigException` naming `message.max.bytes`. |
| whole cluster | 10:13 | Two healthy brokers remained, so each partition kept a second in-sync copy and producers carried on. No page yet: under-replication has to persist ten minutes before anyone is woken. |
| kafka-02 | 10:17 | Its five-minute pause over, the tool repeated the same steps on the next broker, with the same result. |
| producers | 10:17 | One surviving broker cannot provide two in-sync copies (`min.insync.replicas=2`), so every write asking for `acks=all` was rejected. |
| ledger-service | 10:17 | `LEDGER-E455` logged once per ledger entry that could not go out; entries moved to its retry queue and were retried with growing pauses. |
| on-call | 10:19 | Paged for producer failures. |
| on-call | 10:20 | Halted the run. The remaining broker would have been touched at 10:22. |
| kafka-01, kafka-02 | 10:25 | Last known-good `server.properties` pushed back to just these two; brokers started by hand. |
| whole cluster | 10:27 | Both brokers serving; producers succeed again. |
| ledger-service | 10:28 | Retry queue empty. |
| whole cluster | 10:36 | Every partition fully replicated. Closed. |

## Notes

**The bad value.** Kafka parses `message.max.bytes` as an integer count of bytes. Whoever wrote the change wanted roughly ten megabytes and typed `message.max.bytes=10MB`; the parser refuses the suffix and the broker aborts during startup. Ten mebibytes written correctly is 10485760.

**Why the tool saw success.** systemd treats our broker unit as up the instant its process is spawned, so a restart returns 0 even when the JVM is about to abort on its configuration. In August the tool trusted that return code alone, paused for a fixed time and moved on; nothing asked whether a broker had actually rejoined the cluster. Two brokers were gone before a human was involved.

**Effect on each Kafka user.**

| Service | Effect |
|---|---|
| ledger-service | Published nothing for ten minutes and lost nothing. Its retry queue peaked at about 1,200 entries and was empty by 10:28. CPU unchanged. |
| orders-api | Customers could check out the whole time. Order events go to the outbox first; publishing paused, then resumed with a backlog of about 2,400 events and caught up. |
| notification-worker | Idle: with no new messages arriving, it had nothing to fall behind on. |

## Follow-ups

- team-platform: health-check each broker after its push, so a config run halts on the first broker that does not come back.
- Change review: byte-valued Kafka settings must be bare integers; add a lint for unit suffixes.
- On-call note: a halted run is never resumed as-is; the corrected file goes out as a fresh run.
resolution: The run was stopped before the third broker, the previous server.properties was pushed to kafka-01 and kafka-02, and both were started; all replicas were back in sync at 10:36.
root_cause: The rollout tool pushed message.max.bytes=10MB to server.properties; Kafka needs a plain byte count, so each broker refused the file at startup while systemctl restart still exited 0.
symptoms: kafka-01 and kafka-02 exited at startup after a config push; with one broker left, acks=all producers failed and ledger-service queued entries with LEDGER-E455.
title: Pushed Kafka config stopped two brokers

# fraud-scorer-02 throttling, 22 August 2026: what people asked

Collected afterwards from the questions people sent to the risk rota. Severity sev3, 14:02 to 15:22 UTC. Runbooks: RB-002, RB-006.

### What did payments see?

From 14:02, payments-api-01.prod.internal logged `PAYAPI-W0310`: a fraud score did not arrive in time, so the payment went through the static rules instead of the model. Our pager went off at 14:09.

### Why was the scorer slow if its CPU graph was fine?

An average hides bursts. At 14:20 we flipped Grafana's "Container CPU" to throttled periods, and fraud-scorer-02 sat above the 25% mark. In busy stretches the pod burned through its CFS allowance early and then stalled until its next slice. Reading the cgroup counters by hand twice gave the same answer: throttled slices grew in step with total slices.

### Was it the worker-count problem from last year?

No. The older trouble was gunicorn counting the host's cores. Since late May the Deployment pins `WEB_CONCURRENCY=16`, and listing the master's children on fraud-scorer-02 showed 16 processes. Whether the pod lands on a 16-core host or a 32-core one, it gets 16. The count was right; the allowance was simply smaller than what 16 busy processes want during a spike.

### Could it have been memory growth instead?

RB-006 came first, since swelling memory also makes scoring slow. fraud-scorer-02's working set was level, it had not restarted, and feature reads were quick. No sign of cache growth.

### What changed to cause it today?

We do not know yet. The throttling started with the afternoon load. Why that load produced bigger bursts than usual is still open.

### What was the fix?

At 14:48 we gave the Deployment a larger CPU limit and kept its request as it was, so placement stayed put. New pods were all serving by 15:01. At 15:08 fraud-scorer-02 was back below 25% throttled, and payments-api-01 had gone quiet. Closed at 15:22 after a watch.

### Why not add replicas?

RB-002 warns against it. Extra replicas carry the identical 16 processes and the identical cap, so they would be throttled too.

### Why not lower the worker count instead?

It was on the table. Fewer processes would fit the cap, but each pod would handle fewer scores in parallel, and that trade deserves a calmer day than a live page.

### What is still open?

- Find out what made this afternoon's bursts bigger.
- Decide whether the higher cap stays, or whether 16 processes is more than one pod needs.
- Page on throttled share for fraud-scorer, so a calm-looking average never stands alone.
resolution: The CPU limit on the fraud-scorer Deployment was raised, scheduling request as before; throttling fell back under 25% and the fallbacks on payments-api-01 stopped.
root_cause: fraud-scorer-02's 16 workers drew more CPU in bursts than its limit allowed, so the CFS quota ran out early in many periods and the pod was throttled above the 25% line.
symptoms: payments-api-01 logged PAYAPI-W0310 as fraud scores came back late; fraud-scorer-02 had a slow tail while its average CPU looked unremarkable.
title: Questions and answers: fraud-scorer-02 throttled on a Saturday afternoon

# ledger-service release regression, 11 September 2026

sev2 · 13:15 to 13:40 UTC · cause: ledger-service · affected: payments-api · no runbook covers
this

| UTC | Where | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| 13:15 | ledger-service | A new release is serving. Calls from payments-api start coming back `503`. |
| 13:21 | on-call | Paged on payments-api's failed ledger calls. |
| 13:40 | on-call | Release rolled back, previous version serving, no `503` since; closed. |

## What we know and what we don't

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What broke? | Requests handled by the new ledger-service release returned `503` to payments-api. |
| Where? | The errors came from ledger-service-01 and ledger-service-02 while the release was serving. |
| What fixed it? | Rolling the release back to the previous version. |
| Which change in the release? | Not known yet. The diff hasn't been reviewed yet; the cause stays open until it is. |
| Did anything outside ledger-service change? | Nothing we know of. The release is the only change recorded in the window. |
| Why did the release go out at all? | Its pods became Ready. Readiness shows the process is up, not that a ledger call from payments-api succeeds. |
| What did payments-api do with the failures? | It logged each failed ledger call. How each failed call ended for the payment is outside what this table can say. |
| Was the rollback safe? | Nothing so far suggests the release wrote anything the previous version couldn't read. To be confirmed when the diff is reviewed. |

## What made it short

The page came six minutes after the first errors, and the release was the obvious suspect: the
`503`s began with it, and there was no other change to look at. Rolling back needed no
diagnosis of the cause, only the decision to undo it. Finding the actual bug can happen after
the fact, without customers waiting.

## Follow-ups

| Item | Kind |
|---|---|
| Review the release diff and name the change that caused the `503`s | open question |
| A post-deploy smoke call from payments-api's side before the release takes more traffic | proposal |
| Alert on `503` from ledger-service by instance, so a bad instance shows by name | proposal |
| Re-ship the release only after the cause is fixed and a smoke call passes | proposal |
| Add ledger-service to the services whose releases get a short canary pause | proposal |
resolution: The release was rolled back; with the previous version serving again the 503s stopped, and the incident closed at 13:40.
root_cause: A regression in that day's ledger-service release: requests served by the new version failed with 503.
symptoms: From 13:15, after a ledger-service release, ledger-service-01 and ledger-service-02 answered payments-api calls with 503; payments-api logged the failed ledger calls until the rollback.

# Ticket: CPX-W430 from a single card proxy during an egress node patch

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Severity | sev1 |
| Service | card-processor-proxy, with payments-api affected |
| Started | 2026-09-16 19:41 UTC |
| Resolved | 2026-09-16 20:23 UTC |
| Team | team-payments |
| Runbooks | RB-029 (limiter, placement, levers), RB-016 (checked; its retry lever not used) |

**Description.** Card payments failing with `PAYAPI-E1107` at roughly a quarter of the arrival
rate. card-processor-proxy-01 rejects attempts with `CPX-W430`; card-processor-proxy-02 is
absent from the logs.

## Comments

**19:38** · team-platform: the egress node hosting card-processor-proxy-02 is cordoned, then
emptied, ahead of a kernel update.

**19:40** · team-platform: card-processor-proxy-02 evicted. Its replacement is `Pending`.

**19:41** · first `CPX-W430` on card-processor-proxy-01; `PAYAPI-E1107` starts on payments-api.

**19:48** · payments on-call: paged on the `PAYAPI-E1107` rate.

**19:52** · payments on-call: pod listing for the proxy shows -01 Running and the replacement
Pending; the scheduler's event blames anti-affinity plus the egress taint. Only two nodes carry
that taint. One is cordoned and the second already hosts -01.

**19:55** · payments on-call: every rejection comes from card-processor-proxy-01. Processor
latency is normal and the processor is not answering with its own rate-limit reply. Nobody
outside is throttling us; our own limiter is.

**19:58** · payments on-call: the numbers. Payments come in at roughly 240 per second.
One instance gets 180 tokens a second (`CPX_LOCAL_RPS`), and every attempt spends one, retries
included. Each admitted attempt finishes a payment, so at most 180 payments a second get through
and the remaining 240 − 180 = 60 a second use up their attempts and fail. The dashboard shows
about 60 `PAYAPI-E1107` a second. With both instances up the budget is 2 × 180 = 360, well above
the arrivals.

**20:02** · payments on-call: read RB-016 because retries are in the picture. Its first move,
cutting payments-api's attempts per payment down to 1, would not help here. The limiter lets through 180 attempts a
second whatever the attempts per payment, so the same 60 a second would fail, only sooner, and the
processor is not the one pushing back. The attempt setting stays at 3.

**20:06** · payments on-call: RB-029's other lever is raising `CPX_LOCAL_RPS` on -01 to 360 for
as long as it is the only instance. That needs -01 restarted, and since the replacement is
already Pending, a rollout won't remove -01; we would have to delete it ourselves and serve
zero payments until it returned.
Trading a partial outage for a total one: no. We wait for the node.

**20:18** · team-platform: patch applied, node rebooted.

**20:20** · team-platform: node uncordoned.

**20:22** · card-processor-proxy-02 Running and taking traffic.

**20:23** · `CPX-W430` gone, `PAYAPI-E1107` back to its usual level. Resolving.

## Resolution note

Card payments failed at a sustained rate for 42 minutes. We chose to leave `CPX_LOCAL_RPS` and
the attempt setting as they were (see 20:02 and 20:06); the fix was the node coming back.

## For the review

- Cordoning either egress machine is a payments event. Proposal: maintenance on the egress pool
  is announced to team-payments first and done off-peak.
- Open question: should the patch have waited for a quieter hour?
- An alert for `CPX-W430` coming from one instance only, which says an instance is missing, would
  have named the cause at 19:41 instead of at 19:55.
- Pooling the token budget between the two instances is still only a proposal. With it, -01
  alone could have used the full 360.
resolution: The node was uncordoned at 20:20, after the patch and reboot finished at 20:18; card-processor-proxy-02 returned and the rejections stopped at 20:23.
root_cause: The egress node under card-processor-proxy-02 was cordoned for a kernel patch and the replacement pod could not schedule, so proxy-01's local budget of 180 tokens a second met about 240 payment requests a second.
symptoms: From 19:41 card-processor-proxy-01 logged CPX-W430 and payments-api logged about 60 PAYAPI-E1107 a second, while card-processor-proxy-02 was missing.
title: Cordoned egress node left one card proxy with the whole load
